ACV: A modern literal English translation by Walter L. Porter (2005), aimed at conservative Restoration Movement readers. Strives for close word-for-word rendering of the original languages while remaining readable in contemporary English.
AKJV: The American King James Version (Michael Peter Engelbrite, 1999) modernizes the 1769 KJV by replacing archaic pronouns and spellings while preserving its underlying text base. Released into the public domain to encourage free digital distribution.
ASV: The American Standard Version (1901) is the American revision of the English Revised Version, produced by a committee of American scholars during the late 19th century. It became foundational for later 20th-century translations including the RSV and NASB.
Alb: A 19th-century Albanian Protestant translation, associated with Konstandin Kristoforidhi's pioneering work to render the Bible into modern Albanian. His translations helped standardize the Albanian literary language.
Anderson: Henry Tompkins Anderson's 1864 New Testament was among the first American translations from the Greek by a Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement scholar. Anderson worked to produce a fresh rendering unshackled from the KJV tradition.
ArmEastern: The Eastern Armenian Bible reflects the standardized literary Armenian used in the Republic of Armenia and by diaspora communities in Iran, Russia, and elsewhere. It descends from the 5th-century translation attributed to Mesrop Mashtots.
BBE: The Bible in Basic English (1949/1964) was directed by Cambridge scholar S. H. Hooke, using a restricted 850-word Basic English vocabulary developed by C. K. Ogden. Intended to make Scripture accessible to non-native English speakers.
BSB: The Berean Standard Bible (formerly Berean Study Bible), completed in 2020 by Bible Hub, uses a 'optimal equivalence' method aimed at balancing readability with translation transparency. Released into the public domain for unrestricted use.
BeaMRK: The Gospel of Mark translated into Beaver (Danezaa), a Northern Athabaskan language of northeastern British Columbia and northwestern Alberta. Produced as part of missionary linguistic work with First Nations communities.
BurJudson: Adoniram Judson's 1835 Burmese Bible was the fruit of nearly three decades of missionary work in Burma by the American Baptist. It remains the dominant translation among Burmese Christians and shaped the modern literary language.
Byz: The Byzantine Textform 2013 (Robinson-Pierpont) is a Greek New Testament edited from the majority of surviving Greek manuscripts, which reflect the Byzantine text tradition. It represents an alternative to the eclectic Nestle-Aland/UBS text.
CPDV: The Catholic Public Domain Version (Ronald L. Conte Jr., 2009) is a modern English translation from the Clementine Vulgate, released into the public domain. Designed for Catholics who prefer a Vulgate-based text in contemporary English.
CSlElizabeth: The Elizabeth Bible (1751-1757) is the authoritative Church Slavonic Bible of the Russian Orthodox Church, revised under Empress Elizabeth of Russia. It became the standard liturgical text in Slavic Orthodox worship.
CebPinadayag: A Cebuano translation of the Bible in the Visayan language of the central Philippines. Produced to serve the second-largest language community in the country.
Che1860: The Cherokee New Testament of 1860 was printed in the Cherokee syllabary devised by Sequoyah in the early 1820s. Missionary translators worked with Cherokee speakers to produce Scripture in the newly literate written form.
ChiSB: The Studium Biblicum Version (思高本, 1968) is the standard Chinese Catholic Bible, translated by Franciscan biblical scholar Gabriele Allegra and his team in Hong Kong over more than three decades. It renders from the original Hebrew and Greek rather than the Vulgate.
ChiUn: The Chinese Union Version (和合本, 1919) is the dominant Protestant Chinese Bible, produced by a joint committee of missionaries and Chinese scholars from 1890 to 1919. Its influence on modern written Chinese has been compared to that of the KJV on English.
ChiUnL: The Chinese Union Literary Version (文理和合本) renders the Union Bible into 深文理 (deep literary) Classical Chinese rather than Mandarin vernacular. Prepared alongside the vernacular edition to serve traditional literati readers.
CopSahBible2: The Sahidic Coptic Bible preserves early Egyptian Christian Scripture in the Sahidic dialect of Upper Egypt, which was the dominant literary Coptic dialect from the 3rd to 11th centuries. Sahidic witnesses are among the earliest translations of the New Testament.
CroSaric: Ivan Šarić's Croatian Bible (1942), translated by the Archbishop of Sarajevo, was a Catholic rendering completed during World War II. It became widely used among Croatian Catholics and was revised in later editions.
CzeBKR: The Kralice Bible (1579-1594) was the landmark Czech Protestant translation produced by the Unity of the Brethren at Kralice nad Oslavou. Rendered from the original languages, it shaped modern literary Czech.
CzeCSP: The Czech Study Translation (Český studijní překlad, completed 2009) is a modern scholarly Czech translation designed for study. Produced by evangelical scholars working from the original Hebrew and Greek texts.
DRC: The Douay-Rheims Bible (1582 NT, 1609-1610 OT) was the English Catholic translation from the Latin Vulgate produced by exiled English Catholics in France. The Challoner Revision (1749-1752) modernized the language and became the standard Catholic English Bible for two centuries.
DaOT1871NT1907: A composite Danish Bible combining the Old Testament of 1871 with the New Testament of 1907, in original orthography. Represents the authorized Danish Lutheran translation before 20th-century revisions.
Darby: The Darby Bible (1889 English edition) was translated by John Nelson Darby, a founder of the Plymouth Brethren movement. Notable for its extreme literalness and its influence on later dispensationalist Bible study.
DutSVV: The Statenvertaling (1637) is the Dutch Authorized Version, commissioned by the Synod of Dort (1618-19) and translated directly from Hebrew and Greek. It played a role in Dutch culture and language comparable to the KJV in English.
DutSVVA: The Statenvertaling edition including the Apocryphal/Deuterocanonical books, which were originally printed as a separate appendix in the 1637 Dutch Authorized Version.
Esperanto: The Esperanto Bible (Londona Biblio) combines L. L. Zamenhof's Old Testament translation with the New Testament produced by a British committee, published in 1926. Zamenhof, the Polish creator of Esperanto, worked on the OT translation until his death in 1917.
Est: The Estonian Bible traces back to Anton thor Helle's 1739 translation, the first complete Bible in Estonian, produced during the era of Baltic German Lutheran influence. Subsequent editions modernized the language while preserving thor Helle's foundational work.
FinBiblia: The Finnish Biblia of 1776 was the authorized Finnish Lutheran translation used for over 150 years. It built on Mikael Agricola's 16th-century pioneering work and remained the standard until the 1933/1938 revision.
FinPR: The Finnish Pyhä Raamattu (1933 OT / 1938 NT) is the authorized modern Finnish translation of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland. It replaced the 1776 Biblia and served as the standard Finnish Bible for much of the 20th century.
FinSTLK2017: A 2017 literal Finnish translation associated with the STLK (Suomen Tunnustuksellinen Luterilainen Kirkko) confessional Lutheran movement. Emphasizes fidelity to the Textus Receptus and Masoretic tradition.
FreBBB: The Bible Bovet Bonnet (1900) is a French Protestant translation by Swiss scholar Félix Bovet and pastor Louis Bonnet. Produced within the tradition of Neuchâtel Reformed scholarship.
FreBDM1744: David Martin's French Bible (1707, revised 1744) was a Reformed Protestant translation produced by the French refugee community in the Netherlands. It served French-speaking Protestants after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes drove them from France.
FreCrampon: Augustin Crampon's Bible (completed 1904, revised 1923) was the first major French Catholic translation from the original languages rather than the Vulgate. Widely used by French Catholics through the mid-20th century.
FreGeneve1669: The Geneva Bible of 1669 (French New Testament) descends from the Reformed tradition of French Protestant translation centered in Geneva since Olivétan's 1535 rendering. Served the Huguenot community during a period of persecution.
FreJND: J. N. Darby's French Bible was translated by the Plymouth Brethren founder as part of his multilingual literal translation project. Widely used by French-speaking Brethren congregations.
FreLXX: Pierre Giguet's 1872 French translation of the Septuagint (Greek Old Testament), the first substantial French rendering of the LXX. Notable for bringing the Greek Old Testament tradition to French Catholic and academic readers.
FreLXXGiguet: A longer-attributed edition of Pierre Giguet's 1872 French Septuagint translation, produced with additional collaborators. Represents the same base text as FreLXX with fuller editorial context.
FreOltramare1874: Hugues Oltramare's 1874 French New Testament, translated by the Genevan theologian and professor of New Testament exegesis. Reflects 19th-century French Reformed scholarship.
FrePGR: The Perret-Gentil et Rilliet Bible was translated by Swiss Reformed scholars Samuel Robert Louis Perret-Gentil (OT) and Frédéric Rilliet (NT) in the mid-19th century. Produced within the Neuchâtel Protestant tradition.
FreStapfer1889: Edmond Stapfer's 1889 French New Testament was translated by the Reformed theologian and professor at the Faculté de théologie protestante de Paris. Aimed at scholarly and educated French Protestant readership.
FreSynodale1921: The Synodale Version (1921) was the authorized French Reformed New Testament and Psalter, produced under the auspices of French Protestant national synods. It followed earlier 19th-century Reformed translation efforts.
Geneva1599: The Geneva Bible (1560, with the 1599 edition being especially popular) was produced by English Protestant exiles during Mary I's reign. Famous for its extensive marginal notes and its use by the Pilgrims; it was the primary English Bible before the KJV.
GerAlbrecht: Ludwig Albrecht's German New Testament and Psalms (early 20th century) was translated by the Free Church minister with attention to scholarly detail and Pietist devotional readership.
GerBoLut: A modernized-spelling edition of Martin Luther's 1545 Bible, the Reformer's final revision. Luther's translation, first completed in 1534, shaped modern High German more than any other book.
GerElb1871: The Elberfelder Bible (1871) was translated by John Nelson Darby with German Plymouth Brethren collaborators, aiming for the most literal possible rendering of the original languages. Named after the city of Elberfeld where the work was based.
GerElb1905: The 1905 revision of the Darby Elberfelder Bible, prepared by German Brethren scholars after Darby's death. This edition remained the standard 'unrevised' Elberfelder for much of the 20th century.
GerGruenewald: The Grünewald Bibel (1924) was a German Catholic translation prepared for parish use in the interwar period. Notable for its accessible language for lay Catholic readers.
GerLeoNA28: The Leonberger Bibel New Testament, a modern German scholarly translation based on the Nestle-Aland 28th edition Greek text. Produced for study and academic use.
GerMenge: Hermann Menge's German Bible (completed 1926, revised 1939) was translated by the retired classical philologist over three decades. Known for its accuracy and its distinctive parenthetical interpretive glosses.
GerOffBiSt: The Offene Bibel Studienfassung is a collaborative open-source German study Bible translation begun in the 2000s. Produced by a wiki-style community of scholars and volunteers under free-content licensing.
GerSch: Franz Eugen Schlachter's German Bible (1905, revised as the Schlachter 1951) was translated by the Swiss Reformed evangelist. The Schlachter tradition remains popular among German-speaking evangelical and pietist Christians.
GerTafel: Leonhard Tafel's German Tafelbibel (1911) was translated by the Swedenborgian minister. Reflects the New Church interpretive tradition in its rendering choices.
GerTextbibel: The Textbibel des Alten und Neuen Testaments (1906) was a scholarly German translation produced by Emil Kautzsch (OT) and Carl Weizsäcker (NT). Reflected the state-of-the-art historical-critical scholarship of its era.
GerZurcher: The Zürcher Bibel (1931 edition) descends from the Reformed translation begun by Ulrich Zwingli and his Zurich collaborators in the 1520s-1530s, actually completed before Luther's German OT. The 1931 revision modernized the language for 20th-century Swiss Reformed use.
GreVamvas: Neophytos Vamvas's Modern Greek translation (1850) was the first substantial rendering of the whole Bible into vernacular Modern Greek. The Athens University professor's work was controversial with the Orthodox Church, which favored liturgical Koine.
Haitian: The Haitian Creole Bible (Bib la) renders Scripture into the Kreyòl spoken by most Haitians, produced by the Bible Society of Haiti in the late 20th century. It supports religious literacy for speakers who may not read French fluently.
Haweis: Thomas Haweis's 1795 New Testament was translated by the Anglican evangelical clergyman and Selina, Countess of Huntingdon's chaplain. Notable as an early modern English NT translation from the Greek.
HebModern: A Modern Hebrew translation of the New Testament, descending from Franz Delitzsch's 19th-century scholarly rendering. Provided a Hebrew NT for Jewish readers and for Christian study of NT Greek in Semitic idiom.
HunKar: The Revised Károli Bible (1908 edition) is the standard Hungarian Protestant Bible, based on Gáspár Károli's 1590 Vizsoly translation. Károli's original was the first complete Hungarian Bible and remains a cornerstone of Hungarian literary culture.
JPS: The Jewish Publication Society's 1917 Old Testament was the first major English translation of the Hebrew Bible produced by Jewish scholars for Jewish readers. It responded to the perceived Christian bias of prior English versions.
JapBungo: The Meiji Bungo Bible was the classical literary Japanese (文語) translation of the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Produced by missionary and Japanese scholarly committees, it remained influential until postwar colloquial translations displaced it.
JapDenmo: Denmo Seisho (電網聖書) is a modern colloquial Japanese public-domain translation intended for free online distribution. Its name literally means 'electronic-network Bible'.
JapKougo: The Kougo-yaku (口語訳) Bible (1954 OT / 1955 NT) was the first colloquial modern Japanese translation, produced by the Japan Bible Society after WWII. Replaced the Meiji Bungo classical style with contemporary spoken Japanese.
Jubilee2000: Russell M. Stendal's English Jubilee 2000 Bible aims to restore what the translator considered 'original' meanings by reference to the Reina-Valera Spanish tradition. Reflects a distinctive theological approach popular in some evangelical circles.
KJV: The King James Version (1611, standardized in the 1769 Blayney edition) was commissioned by King James I of England at the 1604 Hampton Court Conference to produce a definitive English Bible. Its literary influence on English rivals that of Shakespeare.
KJVA: The King James Version including the Apocryphal/Deuterocanonical books, which were part of the original 1611 KJV publication. Later Protestant editions often omitted them, but many Anglican and academic editions retain them.
KJVPCE: The Pure Cambridge Edition of the KJV is a mid-20th-century Cambridge University Press printing that certain KJV-Only movements consider the definitive standard text. Textually nearly identical to earlier editions but with settled orthographic choices.
KLV: The Klingon Language Version renders the World English Bible into Klingon, the constructed language of the Star Trek Klingon race. A curiosity of fan-driven constructed-language translation projects.
KorHKJV: The Korean Hangul King James Version is a Korean translation aligned with the KJV textual tradition, produced for the Korean KJV-Only community. Uses modern Hangul script.
KorRV: The Korean Revised Version (개역성경, 1961) is the standard Korean Protestant Bible, revised from the earlier Ross and Underwood translations of the late 19th century. Long used by Korean Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist churches.
LEB: The Lexham English Bible (2010) is a modern academic translation produced by Logos Bible Software from a fresh rendering of Greek and Hebrew critical texts. Designed for use alongside original-language study tools.
LITV: Jay P. Green Sr.'s Literal Translation of the Holy Bible (1985) is an extremely word-for-word English rendering, based on the Textus Receptus and Masoretic Text. Widely used for interlinear-style study.
LvGluck8: The 8th edition of Ernst Glück's Latvian Bible, based on the pioneering 1685 translation by the German Lutheran pastor. Glück's Bible is considered a foundational document of Latvian literary culture.
MKJV: Jay P. Green's Modern King James Version (1962) updates the KJV's archaic English while retaining the Textus Receptus and Masoretic base text. Aimed at readers who value the KJV textual tradition but want modernized English.
Mal1910: Sathyavedapusthakam (1910) is the standard Malayalam Bible, produced by the Bible Society of India after decades of missionary-scholar collaboration in Kerala. It shaped modern literary Malayalam among South Indian Christians.
ManxGaelic: Manx Gaelic Scripture portions preserve the Bible translations of the Isle of Man's Celtic language, first fully published in 1775 under Bishop Mark Hildesley. Manx is now a revived language after near-extinction.
Maori: Te Paipera Tapu (the Maori Bible) descends from the missionary translation efforts of the Church Missionary Society in early 19th-century New Zealand, first completed in the 1850s. It played a role in the standardization of written Maori.
MapM: Miqra al pi ha-Mesorah is a modern critical edition of the Hebrew Bible prepared by Mechon Mamre, based on the Aleppo Codex where extant and the Leningrad Codex for missing portions. Produced as a scholarly free-distribution Hebrew text.
Mg1865: The Malagasy Bible of 1865 was completed by the London Missionary Society and Malagasy collaborators during a difficult period of Christian persecution under Queen Ranavalona I. It shaped modern Malagasy literary language.
NHEB: The New Heart English Bible is a public-domain modern English translation derived from the World English Bible tradition, itself descended from the ASV. Produced by volunteer editors for unrestricted distribution.
NHEBJE: The Jehovah Edition of the New Heart English Bible uses 'Jehovah' in the Old Testament wherever the Tetragrammaton appears in Hebrew. Serves readers who prefer that divine-name convention.
NHEBME: The Messianic Edition of the New Heart English Bible uses Hebrew names and Messianic Jewish terminology (e.g., Yeshua, Elohim). Aimed at Messianic Jewish communities.
NlCanisius1939: The Petrus Canisius Bible (1939) was the standard Dutch Catholic translation of the mid-20th century, produced by the Apologetische Vereniging Petrus Canisius. Translated from the original languages under the direction of scholarly Dutch Catholics.
NorSMB: Studentmållagsbibelen (1921) was a Norwegian Nynorsk New Testament translation produced by the Norwegian Students' Language Society. Contributed to the establishment of Nynorsk as a literary standard alongside Bokmål.
Norsk: The Norwegian Bibelselskap Bible of 1930 (Bokmål) was the authorized 20th-century Norwegian Lutheran translation. Served the Church of Norway until subsequent revisions in later decades.
Noyes: George Rapall Noyes's 1869 translation was produced by the Harvard Divinity School Unitarian scholar. Reflects mid-19th-century American liberal Protestant scholarship of the original languages.
OEB: The Open English Bible (US spelling) is a modern public-domain translation based on the early 20th-century Twentieth Century New Testament, revised for contemporary readers. Distributed under free-content licensing.
OEBcth: The Open English Bible in Commonwealth spelling — the same translation as the OEB, adjusted for British/Commonwealth English orthography (e.g., 'colour', 'centre'). Serves non-American English readers.
Peshitta: The Peshitta is the standard Syriac Christian Bible, whose Old Testament portions may date to the 2nd century and New Testament to the 4th or 5th. Long the authoritative text of the Syriac Orthodox, Assyrian, and Maronite churches.
PohnOld: An older public-domain translation of Scripture into Pohnpeian, the language of Pohnpei state in the Federated States of Micronesia. Descends from 19th-century American Board missionary translation work in the Caroline Islands.
PolGdanska: The Gdańsk Bible (1632) was the standard Polish Protestant translation, produced by Polish Reformed scholars including Daniel Mikołajewski in the Baltic port city then a center of Polish Protestantism. The 1881 edition preserves this tradition.
PolUGdanska: The Updated Gdańsk Bible is a 21st-century Polish Protestant revision that modernizes the language of the historic Gdańsk Bible while retaining the Textus Receptus base. Popular in contemporary Polish evangelical circles.
PorBLivre: The Bíblia Livre is a modern Portuguese translation released under free-content licensing for unrestricted distribution. Aims to provide Portuguese-speaking Christians with an open Bible outside proprietary publishing.
PorBLivreTR: A Textus Receptus-based edition of the Bíblia Livre, serving Portuguese-speaking readers who prefer the traditional Greek text of the Reformation era.
PorNVA: The Nova Versão de Acesso Livre is a modern Portuguese translation with an open access license. Produced to support Portuguese Bible study in the digital era.
RLT: A 2018 Revised Literal Translation of the KJV augmented with Strong's numbers and morphology. Intended as a study tool bridging the KJV tradition with the original-language reference systems.
RNKJV: The Restored Name King James Version replaces the divine name and Jesus's name with Hebrew forms (e.g., YHWH, Yahshua) in a KJV base text. Used by Sacred Name movement adherents.
RWebster: Noah Webster's 1833 revision of the KJV was the American lexicographer's attempt to modernize archaic vocabulary and correct what he considered grammatical or moral infelicities. Reflects Webster's project of Americanizing English literature and reference works.
Rotherham: Joseph Bryant Rotherham's Emphasised Bible (final edition 1902) uses typographic marks to indicate Greek and Hebrew emphasis and word order. A distinctive Victorian-era attempt to convey original-language nuance in English.
RusMakarij: Metropolitan Makarij Glukharev's Russian Pentateuch was a mid-19th-century translation from Hebrew by the pioneering Altai missionary. Long unofficial, it eventually influenced the Russian Synodal translation.
RusSynodal: The Russian Synodal Bible (1876) is the authorized Russian Orthodox translation, completed after decades of debate between vernacular Russian and Church Slavonic advocates. It remains the standard Russian Bible for Orthodox, Protestant, and Catholic readers.
SP: The Samaritan Pentateuch is the Torah preserved by the Samaritan community, differing in ~6,000 places from the Masoretic Text. Written in the Samaritan script, it represents an ancient Hebrew textual tradition parallel to the Jewish transmission.
SloChraska: Antonín Chráska's Slovenian Bible (1914) was a Protestant translation produced by the Czech-Slovene evangelical worker for the small Slovenian Protestant community. Its underlying textual tradition contrasted with the dominant Catholic translations of the era.
SloKJV: A Slovenian translation of the KJV, aligning Slovene-language Scripture with the King James textual tradition. Produced for Slovene Protestants and KJV-tradition sympathizers.
SloOjacano: Slovenian selections (Psalms and Galatians) rendered in the style of the Amplified Bible, with expanded interpretive glosses for study. A partial reference-style Slovenian work.
SloStritar: Josip Stritar's 1882 Slovenian New Testament and Psalms was translated by the Slovene poet and literary figure. Reflects late 19th-century Slovene cultural and linguistic development.
SpaPlatense: Juan Straubinger's Biblia Platense (mid-20th century) was the standard Argentine Catholic Bible, produced by the German-born priest working in La Plata, Argentina. Widely used across Spanish-speaking Latin American Catholicism.
SpaRV: The Reina-Valera 1909 revision is one of the most widely used Spanish Protestant Bibles, descending from Casiodoro de Reina's 1569 translation and Cipriano de Valera's 1602 revision. The Reina-Valera tradition is the Spanish Protestant analogue of the KJV.
SpaRV1865: The 1865 revision of the Reina-Valera Bible, an intermediate step in the ongoing textual updating of the 1569 original. Reflects mid-19th-century Spanish orthographic and stylistic norms.
SpaRVG: The Reina-Valera Gómez (2004, revised subsequently) is a modern revision produced by Humberto Gómez to align the Reina-Valera tradition more closely with the KJV textual base. Popular among some independent Baptist and KJV-Only Spanish-speaking congregations.
SrKDEkavski: The Ekavian Serbian Bible of Đura Daničić (OT) and Vuk Karadžić (NT), completed in the mid-19th century, was a landmark of the vernacular Serbian literary reform. This edition uses the Ekavian dialect of eastern Serbia.
SrKDIjekav: The Ijekavian version of the Daničić-Karadžić Serbian Bible uses the Ijekavian dialect spoken in western Serbia, Bosnia, Herzegovina, and Montenegro. Complements the Ekavian edition for dialect-specific readership.
StatResGNT: The Statistical Restoration Greek New Testament is a modern computationally-produced eclectic Greek NT, using statistical analysis of manuscript witnesses. Represents a novel methodological approach to textual criticism.
Swe1917: The Swedish Bible of 1917 was the authorized Church of Sweden translation of the early 20th century, commissioned by King Gustaf V. Replaced the earlier Karl XII Bible tradition as the standard Swedish Lutheran text.
SweKarlXII: The Karl XII Bible (1703) was the Swedish authorized version produced under King Charles XII, revising the 1541 Gustav Vasa Bible. It remained the standard Swedish Bible until the 1917 revision.
SweKarlXII1873: The 1873 revision of the Karl XII Bible modernized the orthography and some vocabulary while preserving the underlying translation. Served late 19th-century Swedish Lutheran readers.
TR: The Textus Receptus (1550/1894) is the Greek New Testament text tradition compiled by Erasmus (1516), refined by Stephanus (1550), Beza, and Scrivener (1894). Underlies the Reformation-era translations including Luther's German and the English KJV.
TagAngBiblia: The Philippine Bible Society's 1905 Tagalog Bible (Ang Biblia) was the first complete Tagalog Protestant translation. It shaped modern Tagalog Christian vocabulary and remained standard for decades.
Tausug: Kitab Injil in the Tausug language of the Sulu Archipelago in the southern Philippines. Produced to serve the predominantly Muslim Tausug community with Christian scriptures.
ThaiKJV: A Thai translation aligned with the KJV textual tradition, produced for Thai Protestants who prefer the underlying Received Text. Complements Bible Society of Thailand editions based on critical texts.
TpiKJPB: King Jems Pisin Baibel translates the KJV into Tok Pisin, the English-based creole widely spoken in Papua New Guinea. Serves Tok Pisin-speaking Christians in a KJV-Only tradition.
Twenty: The Twentieth Century New Testament (1904, revised 1904) was a pioneering effort to produce a modern-English NT from the Westcott-Hort Greek text. Prepared by a committee of ~35 Anglo-American Christians of varying denominations.
Tyndale: William Tyndale's Bible (NT 1526, revised 1534; partial OT 1530-1531) was the first English translation from the original Greek and Hebrew rather than Latin. Tyndale was executed for heresy in 1536, but his rendering shaped the KJV and the English language itself.
UKJV: The Updated King James Version is a modernization of the KJV vocabulary while preserving its textual base and phrasing where readable. Aims to make the KJV accessible without abandoning its tradition.
UkrOgienko: Ivan Ohienko's Ukrainian Bible (completed 1962, published in full 1963) was translated by the Metropolitan of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church in Canada. It is the standard Ukrainian Bible for Protestants and many Orthodox readers.
Viet: The Vietnamese Bible of 1934 (Cadman-Phan Khôi translation) was produced by American Bible Society missionary William Cadman and Vietnamese scholar Phan Khôi. It shaped Vietnamese Protestant vocabulary and remained standard for generations.
VulgClementine: The Clementine Vulgate (1592, revised 1593 and 1598) was Pope Clement VIII's authorized edition of the Latin Vulgate for the Catholic Church. It replaced the flawed Sixtine Vulgate of 1590 and remained the Church's official Latin text until Vatican II.
VulgConte: The edition of the Clementine Vulgate published by Michele Amelli, Aloisio Gramatica, and Alberto Conte in the early 20th century. A widely-used Catholic scholarly printing of the Clementine text.
VulgHetzenauer: The Clementine Vulgate edited by Michael Hetzenauer (Innsbruck, 1906), a Franciscan biblical scholar. Long considered a reliable critical edition of the Clementine text for academic and ecclesiastical use.
VulgSistine: The Sixtine Vulgate (1590) was Pope Sixtus V's ill-fated attempt to produce a definitive Latin Bible. Its many errors led to its being quickly withdrawn after Sixtus's death and superseded by the Clementine edition of 1592.
Vulgate: The Latin Vulgate is Jerome's late 4th-century translation of the Bible into Latin, produced 382-405 at Pope Damasus I's commission. It became the standard Bible of Western Christianity for over a millennium.
WLC: The Westminster Leningrad Codex is the digital critical edition of the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), the oldest complete Masoretic Hebrew Bible manuscript. Serves as the base text of most modern Hebrew Bible editions and translations.
Webster: Noah Webster's 1833 revision of the KJV modernized certain archaic terms and corrected what the American lexicographer considered errors or improprieties. Part of Webster's broader project to Americanize English literature.
Wulfila: The Gothic Bible was translated in the 4th century by Bishop Wulfila (Ulfilas), an Arian Christian missionary to the Goths, using an alphabet he invented for the Gothic language. It is the earliest substantial extant text in any Germanic language.
Wycliffe: The Wycliffe Bible (c. 1382-1395) was the first complete English Bible, translated from the Latin Vulgate by followers of John Wycliffe. Its production was declared heretical and possession banned, but manuscripts circulated widely among the Lollards.
YLT: Robert Young's Literal Translation (1862, revised 1898) aims for an extremely literal English rendering that preserves original-language tense and idiom. Young, a Scottish self-taught orientalist, also compiled the well-known Analytical Concordance.
sml_BL_2008: Kitab Awal-Jaman maka Kitab Injil (2008) is a Bible portion translation in the Central Sama (Sama Bangingi) language of the Sulu Archipelago. Serves a small Austronesian language community in the southern Philippines and eastern Malaysia.
vlsJoNT: Nicolaas De Jonge's New Testament in West Flemish is a 19th-century rendering of the NT into the Flemish dialect spoken in West Flanders. Produced during the era of Flemish literary revival within Belgium.
